subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage:
Hemant: Omkar, I am at the hardware shop and the owner only speaks Bengali. I need a hinge for the cupboard
Omkar: Show him the broken one
Hemant: I did. Then I drew a little door with my finger, opening and closing 😅
Omkar: And?
Hemant: He gave me a lock. Wrong thing
Omkar: Take a photo of the hinge and show it, then say "this one" and point
Hemant: Good idea. Also he nodded in a way I could not read. Yes or no?
Omkar: Ask again with the photo
Hemant: Done. He is smiling and opening a drawer. Fingers crossed 🤞

qa.q: What did Hemant need from the hardware shop?
qa.a: He needed a hinge for the cupboard.

qa.q: Why was Hemant unsure about the owner's nod, and what did he feel?
qa.a: He could not read whether the nod meant yes or no, and he was uneasy after being handed the wrong item. The nod might have been polite or confirming, so he wanted to check.

qa.q: What did Omkar suggest to avoid another mistake?
qa.a: He suggested showing a photo of the hinge and saying "this one" while pointing, so the request is confirmed with an image.

qa.q: How might the shop owner have felt when Hemant mimed a door?
qa.a: He may have felt willing to help but uncertain what Hemant wanted, which is why he offered a lock instead.

grounding: Chat about a worker in a new city using shapes, mime and pointing to make a request and checking with a photo to avoid mix-ups.

subtype: Describing with hands to bridge language gaps [Regulating]
passage: Kamal had just started at the brick kiln outside Ranchi, and his Hindi was thin. On his second morning he needed a wheelbarrow with a flat tyre swapped. He pointed at the wheel, made a hissing sound and spread his hands to show air going out. The foreman, Rukmini's uncle, understood and waved him toward the shed. But when Kamal drew a circle in the air to mean "wheel", the man beside him thought he meant the whole team should circle up. They laughed together. Kamal took out his phone, showed a picture of the tyre and said, "Yeh?" The uncle nodded. "Haan, yeh." The tyre was changed within minutes.

qa.q: Where did Kamal start work?
qa.a: He started at a brick kiln outside Ranchi.

qa.q: What did Kamal's picture and "Yeh?" show about his thinking?
qa.a: It showed he wanted to be sure the request was understood, since his air circle had been misread. The laughing suggests the mix-up was harmless.

qa.q: What worked to make his request clear?
qa.a: A phone picture of the tyre and the confirming word "Yeh?" made the request clear after the gestures caused confusion.

qa.q: How might the man beside Kamal have understood the circle in the air?
qa.a: He thought Kamal meant the team should circle up, so he took the gesture as a call to gather.

grounding: Third-person rural narrative of a worker in a new place using mime and pointing that can mislead, confirmed with an image.

passage: Okay Payal, you asked about video calls. Let me tell you about Tuesday. I am Indu, the designer. I was describing a banner, and I held my hands about this wide, a big rectangle, and said, "Something like this." Nobody reacted. Turned out my camera cropped everything below my chin. The client's video also froze right as she used her hands, so I have no idea what shape she meant. I laughed and said, "Sorry, I am waving invisible boxes." Then I typed 'A4 landscape' in the chat and shared my screen with a quick sketch. Everyone got it in seconds. Now I say the size in words first, gesture second.

qa.q: What did Indu type in the chat?
qa.a: She typed "A4 landscape" in the chat.

qa.q: Why did Indu laugh and say she was waving invisible boxes?
qa.a: She realised the camera cropped her hands so nobody could see the shape, and she wanted to lighten the awkward silence. The client's frozen video also meant she may have missed the client's gesture.

qa.q: What could Indu do next time a shape or size matters on a call?
qa.a: She could say the size in words, share her screen or make a quick sketch, as she did, and use gestures only as extra.

qa.q: How might the client have felt watching Indu's cropped video?
qa.a: The client may have felt unsure what Indu meant, since Indu's hands were invisible and the silence left both sides guessing.

grounding: Spoken monologue by a young professional whose gestures are cropped or delayed on video calls, solved by adding words and a shared sketch.

passage: I sat next to Chetan during the client call on Wednesday, so I saw both screens. Chetan held his hands wide, showing how large the packaging box should be, and the client on the screen just nodded blankly. Chetan looked pleased, but the client's face was frozen mid-nod for a second, so I could not tell if she understood. Then the client asked, "Sorry, how big?" Chetan looked surprised. I am Leela, and I leaned over and typed the measurement into the chat. The client wrote back, "Perfect, thank you." I think Chetan believed his hands were enough, but on camera they were cut off.

qa.q: Who typed the measurement into the chat?
qa.a: Leela typed the measurement into the chat.

qa.q: What did Chetan probably believe when the client nodded?
qa.a: He probably believed his hands had shown the size clearly and the client understood, and his pleased look fits that. The frozen nod meant the client might not have seen the shape.

qa.q: What could Chetan do on future calls to avoid this?
qa.a: He could add the measurement in words, type it in the chat or share a quick sketch.

qa.q: How might the client have felt when she asked "Sorry, how big?"
qa.a: She may have felt slightly awkward for interrupting, but relieved once the measurement was written in the chat.

grounding: Observer's account of a young professional's hand descriptions failing on camera, fixed by adding words in the chat.

passage:
Dear Leela,

You asked me last week why I look like a question mark at my desk. Honestly, I have been hunched over the laptop for hours, chin forward, neck and back aching by evening. My manager may think I am deeply focused, but the truth is I am often exhausted and just forgot to move. I have raised the screen on two books and set the chair lower, and I now stand up every hour to fill my water bottle and walk to the window. It has helped my mood too. I only hope nobody reads slouching as laziness. Would you like to join me for the noon walk? 🙂

Chetan

qa.q: What did Chetan put under the laptop screen?
qa.a: Chetan raised the screen on two books.

qa.q: What do Chetan's hunched posture and the letter suggest about the feeling behind it?
qa.a: Chetan is often exhausted and forgot to move, not simply focused. Others might read the posture as focus, but Chetan suspects some might think it is laziness.

qa.q: What small steps helped Chetan feel better?
qa.a: Chetan raised the screen, lowered the chair and stood up every hour to walk to the window, which also helped the mood.

qa.q: How might Chetan's manager see the posture?
qa.a: The manager may take it as deep focus, but might also misread it as tiredness or laziness, since the posture alone does not say which.

grounding: Letter from a young worker who hunches over a laptop, read as focus or exhaustion, and who uses movement, a raised screen and breaks.

passage: So my back, Divyansh. You asked. I am Binita, I work in accounts, and last winter I hunched over my laptop nine hours a day. People said, oh she is so dedicated. Truth? I was tired, my neck was stiff and my mood was flat. One evening my sister said, "You look like a bent spoon." I laughed, then I thought about it. I got a proper chair cushion, moved the laptop up, and started a two-minute stretch every hour. Small things. My colleagues, some of them, had assumed I was lazy when I sank into my chair, and that annoyed me. But it was posture, not attitude. Take the breaks. Your body is not a machine. 🙂

qa.q: What did Binita's sister say she looked like?
qa.a: Her sister said she looked like a bent spoon.

qa.q: How did Binita feel about being called dedicated, and what was the truth?
qa.a: She was tired, with a stiff neck and flat mood, so the praise missed her real state. She was also annoyed that some colleagues read her slump as laziness.

qa.q: What changes helped Binita?
qa.a: She used a chair cushion, raised the laptop and did a two-minute stretch every hour.

qa.q: How might Binita's colleagues have seen her sinking into the chair?
qa.a: Some of them assumed she was lazy, though her posture came from tiredness and discomfort.

grounding: Spoken monologue of a young worker hunched over a laptop for hours, read by others as focus or laziness, helped by movement and breaks.

passage:
"He leaned back the whole time," Aparna said, dropping her bag on the sofa. "Feet on the chair, hands behind his head. Is my new boss bored with me?"

"Or he is comfortable," Akash said. "What was he like when you spoke?"

"He asked good questions. And he remembered my old project."

"So maybe leaning back is just how he is. My old boss stood right over people's desks and it was only because his own chair was broken."

"Ha. But last office, the manager sat upright, very formal."

"Different offices, different habits."

"I will watch what he does over a few weeks instead of guessing."

qa.q: What did Aparna's new boss do with his feet?
qa.a: He had his feet on the chair.

qa.q: What was Aparna worried about, and how did Akash's questions change her view?
qa.a: She worried her boss was bored with her, but Akash pointed out he asked good questions and remembered her project. That evidence suggests leaning back may just be his style.

qa.q: What is a sensible way for Aparna to judge her boss's attitude?
qa.a: She can watch how he behaves over a few weeks instead of guessing from posture alone.

qa.q: How might the boss see his own posture?
qa.a: He may simply feel comfortable and not realise it looks casual or bored to a new employee.

grounding: Dialogue about a young professional meeting a boss who leans back, where posture signals status differently across offices and behaviour over time tells more.

passage: My first job, in Nairobi, was under a manager who sat tall and still, and I thought she was cold. My second, in Chennai, had a boss who leaned back and talked to me with his hands behind his head, and I first felt disrespected. I am Suraj, and I have spent a while working out what posture actually means. Nothing certain, I found. The tall manager turned out to be shy and gave generous feedback. The leaning boss was laid-back but sharp, and fully supportive when I made mistakes. When a third boss stood close beside my desk, I paused before deciding it was pushy. Naveen, my mentor, told me, "Watch what people do over time." That advice saved me from a lot of wrong guesses.

qa.q: Where was Suraj's first job?
qa.a: His first job was in Nairobi.

qa.q: What did Suraj feel about each boss at first, and what was the truth?
qa.a: He felt the tall manager was cold and the leaning boss was disrespectful. In time the manager turned out to be shy and generous, and the leaning boss was laid-back and supportive.

qa.q: What advice helped Suraj avoid wrong guesses?
qa.a: His mentor Naveen said to watch what people do over time.

qa.q: How might the leaning boss have seen his own posture?
qa.a: He probably saw it as relaxed and comfortable, not as a sign of status or disrespect.

grounding: First-person account of a young professional whose bosses lean back, sit tall or stand close, learning that posture alone is a poor guide.

subtype: Restless pacing at work or in waiting rooms [Regulating]
passage: The bad-weather delay had made it worse. Rehana had walked into the clinic waiting room an hour early for her job interview, and now the rain drummed the window and the receptionist said the panel was running behind. She got up and began pacing the corridor, up to the window, back to the poster of vaccination dates, up again. A stranger on the bench, Zainab, watched her. "Looks like you are burning off a lot," she said. Rehana laughed shakily. "Nerves." "Step outside under the porch for a minute," Zainab suggested. "Fresh air. Breathe slowly." Rehana did, and when she came back her shoulders had dropped a little.

qa.q: Why was Rehana at the clinic?
qa.a: She was there for her job interview, an hour early.

qa.q: What did Rehana's pacing suggest about how she felt, and how might others have read it?
qa.a: It suggested nerves about the interview, which she confirmed. Others might have read it as impatience about the delay, but Zainab guessed it was nervous energy.

qa.q: What small step helped Rehana?
qa.a: She stepped under the porch for fresh air and slow breathing, and her shoulders dropped.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt watching Rehana pace?
qa.a: She likely felt kind concern and wanted to help, since she spoke gently and gave a practical suggestion.

grounding: Third-person narrative with a rain delay about a young professional pacing to burn nervous energy before an interview, helped by fresh air and slow breathing.

subtype: Restless pacing at work or in waiting rooms [Regulating]
passage: Ganga's phone buzzed twice and both times she stood up. The doctor's office was on the fourth floor of a Delhi building, and the results of her father's tests were due today. She paced from the water cooler to the notice board and back. Farhan, the office assistant, watched from behind the counter. He wondered if she was impatient with the wait, but her hands were shaking a little, so he guessed she was worried. He asked, "Would you like to sit near the window? Or I can bring water." Ganga took the water and stood by the window instead, breathing slowly. "Thank you," she said. "Walking helps a bit."

qa.q: On which floor was the doctor's office?
qa.a: The doctor's office was on the fourth floor.

qa.q: What did Farhan think Ganga's pacing meant, and what made him change his guess?
qa.a: He first wondered whether she was impatient, then noticed her shaking hands and guessed she was worried about her father's test results. Both readings were possible.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that helped her?
qa.a: She took the water, stood by the window and breathed slowly, using a little walking to ease her nerves.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt about Farhan's offer?
qa.a: She seems to have felt grateful and eased, since she thanked him and accepted the water.

grounding: Third-person urban narrative of a person pacing while waiting for news, read as impatience or worry, helped by water and slow breathing.

subtype: Walking away in conflict at work [Regulating]
passage: I nearly said something I could not take back. In the packing room yesterday, my supervisor's remark about my mistake in front of the whole line made my face burn, and I felt my voice getting loud. I am Shankar, and I have learned my own warning signs by now. So I said, "I need a minute," picked up my water bottle and walked out to the yard. I stood there and breathed for maybe ten minutes. I was afraid it would look like disrespect, honestly. When I came back I said, "I did not want to argue in front of everyone. Can we talk about the label mistake after the shift?" Lokesh, the supervisor, nodded slowly. "Fair. I was harsh."

qa.q: Where did Shankar go on leaving the packing room?
qa.a: Shankar went out to the yard.

qa.q: What was Shankar afraid of when walking out, and what was Shankar feeling?
qa.a: Shankar felt the face burn and feared saying something that could not be taken back, and also worried that leaving would look like disrespect. The plain words on return show a wish to repair, not run away.

qa.q: What made Shankar's leaving work well?
qa.a: Shankar explained why, took a short break, came back and suggested a calm time to talk.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have first seen Shankar walking out?
qa.a: Lokesh might have seen the exit as rude or defiant at first, but the explanation and the return led to an admission of being harsh.

grounding: First-person account of a young worker who leaves the room during a heated exchange, returns and speaks calmly.

subtype: Walking away in conflict at work [Regulating]
passage: Supervisor's note, Friday. I am Ankita, and I saw the following in the print shop. During a disagreement over deadlines, Francis raised his voice, then stopped and said, "I am going to step out for a few minutes, I will be back." He walked out and stood in the lane by the loading bay. The other worker looked confused and a little offended. After about a quarter of an hour Francis returned and said calmly, "I did not want to say something unfair. Can we start again on the schedule?" They did. I noted that the walk seemed to help, and that the explanation mattered. I will check next week whether the pattern holds.

qa.q: Where did Francis stand during his break?
qa.a: He stood in the lane by the loading bay.

qa.q: What did Francis probably feel before he stepped out, and what did the other worker feel?
qa.a: Francis was probably angry and did not want to say something unfair, and the other worker looked confused and a little offended. The stepping out could have been read as disrespect, but his explanation clarified it.

qa.q: What made Francis's exit constructive?
qa.a: He said he would be back, took a short walk, returned and offered to restart the conversation calmly.

qa.q: How might the other worker have seen the exit without the explanation?
qa.a: They might have taken it as disrespect or avoidance, since walking out mid-argument can look dismissive.

grounding: Supervisor's note on a young worker leaving the room during a heated exchange, followed by a return and a calm word.

passage: Kashish here. Last month at the railway station in Pune, a crowd began to push toward the train doors and a young mother stood beside me with a small child. Without thinking, I stepped between the child and the crowd, put an arm out, and told the mother, "Let us wait here by the pillar." Sachin, my friend, was with me and called the station guard over. The guard moved people back, and we took the child aside. Later I felt shaky. I wondered, was blocking the crowd smart? I think moving the child away and calling the guard was better than standing my ground. I was scared but glad to help.

qa.q: Who called the station guard?
qa.a: Sachin, Kashish's friend, called the guard.

qa.q: What did Kashish feel after the crowd moved, and what did Kashish wonder?
qa.a: Kashish felt shaky and scared, but glad to help, and wondered whether blocking the crowd had been smart. The doubt shows an awareness of the risk of standing firm.

qa.q: Which choice worked best in this situation, and why?
qa.a: Moving the child aside and calling the station guard worked best, because it avoided a confrontation and let someone with authority manage the crowd.

qa.q: How might the young mother have felt when Kashish stepped in?
qa.a: The young mother may have felt relieved and protected, though possibly startled since Kashish moved so suddenly.

grounding: Spoken monologue about a young adult shielding a child from a crowd and choosing to move away and call the station guard.

passage: We were outside the hostel gate when a stranger began shouting at Kalyani and would not leave. I am Arnab's roommate; I live two floors above. What I saw was Arnab stepping between Kalyani and the man, with his palm out, telling her, "Go inside." She walked in. Then Arnab backed toward the gate himself and called the warden instead of arguing. The man muttered and left before the warden came. I do not know what the man wanted, and I cannot say what Arnab felt, though his hands were shaking a little afterwards. I think he did the right thing by not arguing, but he could have been hurt.

qa.q: Where did the incident happen?
qa.a: It happened outside the hostel gate.

qa.q: What might Arnab's shaking hands have shown, and what else could they mean?
qa.a: They probably showed fear or adrenaline after the confrontation, though the narrator cannot be sure. They could also have been simple tension after the shock.

qa.q: What made Arnab's response safer?
qa.a: He told Kalyani to go inside, backed away instead of arguing and called the warden.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have felt when Arnab stepped in front of her?
qa.a: She probably felt protected but may also have been scared, since the man was shouting at her and she went inside quickly.

grounding: Observer's account of a young adult shielding a friend from a threat and choosing to move away and call the warden.

passage:
Week 1. Zainab returned to the hospital lab after the long stretch of night shifts and the family loss. Aditi noticed she kept her eyes down, spoke little and flinched when a tray clattered. Aditi decided not to ask anything.

Week 3. Zainab ate lunch alone, looking at the wall. Aditi sat two tables away and said quietly, "I am around if you want company, no need to talk." Zainab gave a small nod.

Week 5. Zainab stayed after her shift and told Aditi she had been struggling and had made an appointment with the hospital counsellor. Aditi said, "I am glad. I will cover the Saturday sample run."

qa.q: What did Zainab make an appointment with?
qa.a: She made an appointment with the hospital counsellor.

qa.q: What might Zainab's downcast eyes and flinching have shown, and what did Aditi do about it?
qa.a: They might have shown stress, grief or exhaustion after the night shifts and the family loss. Aditi did not push and offered company without pressure.

qa.q: What did Aditi do that helped?
qa.a: She stayed patient, offered company without talk and covered a Saturday sample run when Zainab was ready.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt in week 3 when Aditi offered company?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved that no one pressed her, or still unready to talk, since she gave only a small nod.

grounding: Before, during and after account of a young professional who withdraws after a hard period, met with patience and later professional help.

passage: When I was a young clerk, Kamal, I saw it in Rukmini. Elder here. She used to be quick and cheerful, then after the floods and her mother's illness she went quiet, avoided looking at people and jumped when a door banged. Some said she had turned proud. I did not think so. I sat by her at lunch and said nothing about it. Weeks later she said, "I cannot sleep. I do not know why I am so tired." I told her that sounded heavy and that a counsellor could help, and I went with her the first time. I still cannot say what exactly she was going through. But it was not pride.

qa.q: What did Rukmini say she could not do?
qa.a: She said she could not sleep.

qa.q: How did others read Rukmini's withdrawal, and what did the elder think instead?
qa.a: Some said Rukmini had turned proud, but the elder thought it came from hard events like the floods and the mother's illness. The elder could not be sure what Rukmini was feeling, so stayed patient.

qa.q: What approach helped Rukmini?
qa.a: The elder sat with her without pressing her, and later suggested a counsellor and went with her the first time.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt when colleagues called her proud?
qa.a: She may have felt misunderstood and lonelier, since her quietness came from strain and not from pride.

grounding: Elder's account of a young colleague who withdraws and startles after a hard period, met with patience and professional help.

passage: On the tram in Rotterdam, Tuan checked his phone for the third time in ten minutes. Across from him sat Tomas, an old friend visiting for the weekend, halfway through a story about his mother's illness. Tuan's thumb scrolled without reading. His stomach felt tight; he was waiting for a message about his own job contract and could not concentrate. Tomas trailed off. "Am I boring you?" he asked, and Tuan flushed. He put the phone away. "No. I am sorry. I am waiting for news on my contract and my hands keep reaching for it. Your mother matters. Please, go on." Tomas nodded, and this time the story was heard properly.

qa.q: What was Tomas talking about when Tuan checked his phone?
qa.a: Tomas was talking about his mother's illness.

qa.q: Why did Tuan keep reaching for his phone, and how did Tomas read it?
qa.a: Tuan was anxious about his contract and could not concentrate, and Tomas read it as boredom. Both readings were possible until Tuan explained.

qa.q: What helped repair the moment?
qa.a: Tuan put the phone away, explained what he was waiting for and asked Tomas to go on.

qa.q: How might Tomas have felt when Tuan scrolled during his story?
qa.a: He probably felt unimportant or hurt, since he trailed off and asked if he was boring Tuan.

grounding: Third-person narrative set abroad about a young adult fiddling with a phone from anxiety, read as disrespect, resolved by a short explanation.

passage: Community centre meeting notes, as I saw them. During Madhav's presentation on the new library timings, Darshan kept looking at his phone under the table, tapping, scrolling, locking the screen, unlocking it again. Madhav faltered and looked at the floor. After the meeting I asked Darshan what was going on. He said, "My sister's exam results were due and I could not sit still. I should have said so." He then went to Madhav and explained. Madhav said, "I thought I was losing you." They both laughed a little. Nobody can tell from the tapping alone whether someone is bored, anxious or dealing with something urgent.

qa.q: What was Madhav presenting?
qa.a: He was presenting the new library timings.

qa.q: What was Darshan probably feeling while tapping the phone, and what did Madhav think it meant?
qa.a: It came from worry about his sister's exam results, and Madhav read it as losing his audience. This shows the same habit can look like disrespect when it is anxiety.

qa.q: What could Darshan have done to prevent the misunderstanding?
qa.a: He could have quietly said before the meeting that he was waiting for urgent news, or stepped out to check his phone.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt during the presentation?
qa.a: He probably felt discouraged and unsure, since he faltered and looked at the floor when Darshan kept checking the phone.

grounding: Institutional scene of a young adult fiddling with a phone from worry, read as disrespect, cleared up by a short explanation.

subtype: Rubbing temples and neck at work [Expressing]
passage: Jomon had been at the panchayat office since eight, poring over ration lists with the sarpanch and three clerks. By noon he kept pressing his fingers against his temples, then rubbing the back of his neck, then closing his eyes for a moment. Avni, a clerk, saw it and could not tell whether he was tired, tense or had a headache. Instead of guessing, she said, "Jomon-ji, shall we take tea outside for a bit?" He nodded gratefully. Outside, he stretched his neck and said, "Too many numbers." After tea he returned and checked the lists more slowly. Avni was glad she asked.

qa.q: What lists was Jomon reading?
qa.a: He was poring over ration lists.

qa.q: What might Jomon's temple rubbing have meant, and what did Avni do?
qa.a: It could have meant tiredness, tension or a headache, and Avni could not tell which, so she asked kindly and offered tea. Jomon confirmed it was too many numbers.

qa.q: What made Avni's approach useful?
qa.a: She offered a break instead of guessing, which let Jomon rest and return more clearly.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Avni suggested tea?
qa.a: He seems to have felt grateful and relieved, since he nodded gratefully and stretched his neck outside.

grounding: Third-person rural narrative of a young professional rubbing temples and neck in a long meeting, with a colleague offering a break instead of guessing.
